Q116244316.summary: A continuous frieze of closely packed figures in tunics and togas runs along the front of this marble sarcophagus. Near the centre Christ rides a donkey into Jerusalem, with a figure in a tree above and a youth spreading a garment before him; to the right, baskets of loaves stand at the feet of the apostles, and at the far right Lazarus, wrapped like a mummy, stands in the doorway of a temple-fronted tomb. At the left, soldiers in flat caps lead a bearded man away, a scene usually read as the arrest of Peter. Such sarcophagi show how quickly, in the decades after Constantine, Roman sculptors turned the Gospel into a language of salvation for the dead.
facts: The Met dates the sarcophagus to the early 300s and notes that it has undergone modern restoration.
It measures 67.3 × 212.1 × 61.9 cm and was given to the Museum by Josef and Marsy Mittlemann in 1991.

links.label: The Met: Sarcophagus with Scenes from the Lives of Saint Peter and Christ

Q116244316.notes: Scene identifications (Entry into Jerusalem, Multiplication of the Loaves, Raising of Lazarus, Arrest of Peter, and at the far left probably Peter's miracle of the spring with a kneeling soldier drinking) are read from the visible iconography; the Met's online label text was not available. Some heads and details are modern restorations.

cur:monumental-sma-way-to-calvary.summary: Against a dark blue ground, the haloed Christ in a dark robe is led away among soldiers, while at the right a figure (Simon of Cyrene) bears the cross. Only the central part of the panel survives, but the solemn frontal face of Christ amid the crowd still conveys the gravity of the procession to Golgotha.
facts: Santa Maria Antiqua in the Roman Forum preserves wall paintings from the 6th to the late 8th century; buried after an earthquake in 847, it was rediscovered only in 1900.
The Passion scenes in Santa Maria Antiqua include a monumental Christ crucified on the triumphal arch, painted under John VII.

cur:monumental-bawit-baptism.summary: This faded early photograph records a painting of the Baptism of Christ from one of the Bawit chapels: a central haloed figure stands in the waters of the Jordan with figures at either side. Although the details are hard to make out, it documents a lost Coptic image of the Baptism from the monastery's most prosperous period.
facts: The monastery of Apa Apollo at Bawit, founded c. 385/390, flourished in the 6th and 7th centuries; Jean Clédat of the French Institute of Oriental Archaeology excavated its painted 'chapels' from 1901, and many paintings were later removed or lost.
This photograph is an early 20th-century glass lantern slide from the Paris 'Archives photographiques', a record of the painting as excavated.
cur:monumental-bawit-baptism.notes: The photograph is faint; the identification as the Baptism of Christ follows the caption on the slide ('Le baptême du Christ, fresque'). The painting's present whereabouts are not known to us.

cur:objects-berlin-diptych-christ-and-vi.summary: On the left leaf a bearded Christ sits enthroned beneath a shell-headed niche, holding a jewelled book and blessing, flanked by Saints Peter and Paul; on the right leaf the Virgin sits enthroned with the Christ Child on her lap, between two archangels. The two leaves answer each other as the heavenly King and his Mother, each attended by a celestial court. This imperial-looking pair is among the most majestic Christian ivories of the age of Justinian.
facts: Pairing Christ enthroned among apostles with the Virgin enthroned among angels on facing leaves became a model for later Byzantine icon pairs on templon screens (type).
The leaves follow the format of the official consular diptychs of the period, but replace the consul with Christ and the Virgin (type).
cur:objects-berlin-diptych-christ-and-vi.notes: Museum record not accessible; the attribution to Constantinople is the usual one in the literature.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/1galla/2l.summary: In a rocky green landscape beneath a starry blue vault, the young Christ sits among six sheep, reaching across to touch one that turns toward him. He wears a golden tunic with a purple mantle and a golden halo, and holds a tall golden cross instead of a shepherd's crook. The image fuses the gentle shepherd of the Gospel with the majesty of a ruler, one of the most beloved mosaics of the 5th century.
facts: The lunette is set over the north entrance of the building, built between 425 and 450 as a chapel adjoining the church of Santa Croce in Ravenna.
Despite its name, the empress Galla Placidia was not buried here; she died in Rome in 450, and the tradition of her burial in Ravenna dates from the 13th century.
The figure of a shepherd carrying a sheep was adopted from ancient art into Christian funerary art from the late 3rd century; here the shepherd is in imperial purple and gold.
